newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ILO rebukes 20 states for abusing unionists.
newsitem.headline: ILO rebukes 20 states for abusing unionists.

text.p: The International Labour Organisation on Thursday censured 20 countries, including South Korea, where it urged the government to release detained workers and recognise unions with a right to bargain collectively.

In a report, the United Nations agency's freedom of association committee denounced violence against trade unionists -- including murder, disappearances, and intimidation -- in Colombia, Nigeria and Sudan.

The committee urged Brazil to cancel fines imposed on workers for taking part in a 1995 strike at Petrobas oil company and to drop fines in the case of legitimate strike action, while it reprimanded Pakistan for beating up and detaining unionists.

The 226-page report by the ILO's freedom of association committee, which held closed-door meetings earlier this month, was adopted unanimously by the ILO's Governing Body late on Wednesday. The 174-member agency issued the report on Thursday.
The ILO committee oversees compliance with the fundamental principles of freedom of association, which guarantee the right of workers to organise and to engage in collective bargaining.

The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), on behalf of its outlawed member the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU), filed a complaint last December days after South Korea rushed through Parliament amendments to the labour legislation. The Brussels-based ICFTU said these violated previous recommendations of the ILO body.
The ILO body appealed to Seoul to allow it to send a high-level mission to "ensure that ongoing revisions to labour law are consistent with the principles of freedom of association".
The committee urged the government "to take the necessary measures to render trade union pluralism legal without delay".
It called on South Korea to register KCTU, which spearheaded industrial strikes of nearly one month from December to January, as well as the Korean Automobile Workers' Federation.
It was the second time in as many years that the Geneva-based agency, which promotes social justice and global labour standards, reprimanded South Korea, which joined in 1991.
The committee expressed concern over 19 trade union leaders for whom arrest warrants were issued in 1996, and 28 imprisoned and wanted workers who belonged to KCTU affiliated unions.

South Korea's envoy told the ILO committee on Wednesday that only six of the 47 named were serving prison sentences and two were under warrant for arrest, according to diplomatic sources. The rest had been freed, Seoul's delegate said.
South Korea's President Kim Young-sam signed a labour bill into law on March 12 to replace legislation that sparked a wave of strikes after it was rammed through parliament last December.
The new law would permit multiple unions at the national level immediately -- instead of in the year 2000 as in the December law -- and at the company level by the year 2002.
An ILO spokesman told Reuters: "South Korea's legislation is being overhauled in line with ILO principles, according to the government."

"But the legislation is still in the works and has to be reviewed," he added. "The most recent legislative revision is not taken account of in the committee recommendations because the committee did not have the legislation."

In Colombia, the ILO committee said the trade union movement was subject to "serious attacks". It expressed serious concern at the extent of "violent death, disappearances and other acts of violence against trade union officials, as well as raids on trade union headquarters and trade union members' homes".
Trade union rights in Nigeria have been persistently deteriorating since 1994, the committee said. It repeated its long-standing request to visit the country,
It also urged Sudan to guarantee that trade union members were not subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention and sentencing.
